Decreased CSF levels of substance P in 
patients with congenital sensory neuropathy 
with anhidrosis 
Shinichiro Nugumitsu, MD; Toyojiro Matsuishi, MD; 
Akio Ohnishi, MD; and Hirohisa Kato, MD 
Congenital sensory neuropathy with anhidrosis (CSNA) or type IV 
hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy is a rare disease 
characterized by insensitivity to pain, anhidrosis, high fever, self- 
mutilation, and mental retardation. Pathologic findings include a 
markedly decreased number of small myelinated fibers and a vir- 
tual absence of unmyelinated fibers.I However, neither the etiol- 
ogy nor the appropriate treatment in patients with this disease 
has been established. 
The neuropeptide, substance P, is the neurotransmitter of no- 
ciperception at the synapses of primary sensory neurons and is 
contained in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and dorsal spinal 
ganglion neuronal cell bodies,2 but, the role of substance P in 
patients with CSNA has not yet been investigated. The concentra- 
tion of substance P in CSF reflects its concentration in the brain 
and spinal cord.3 Therefore, we measured the CSF levels of sub- 
stance P in patients with this disease and compared the results 
with those levels in controls. 
Methods and Results. A clinical diagnosis of CSNA was con- 
firmed in four patients (aged 0.8 to 3.0 years, mean, 1.52) by sural 
nerve biopsy. Specimens of CSF were obtained with the written 
informed consent of the subjects' parents. Substance P immunore- 
activity was determined by radioimmunoassay using a highly spe-

Figure. CSF substance P levels in patients with congenital 
sensory neuropathy with anhidrosis (CSNA) and control 
groups. Control 1: 10 children who had febrile disorders 
but normal developmental psychomotor milestones. Con- 
trol 2: 10 children who had other neurologic deuelopmen- 
tal disorders. Horizontal bars represent the mean, and 
vertical bars represent the range of the standard error. 
cific anti-substance P serum (supplied by Peninsula Laboratories, 
Belmont, CA, Cat# RAS 7451), which showed no cross-reactivity 
with either neurokinin A or neurokinin B. The CSF substance P 
levels were measured as described previ~usly.~ The mean CSF 
substance P level in these patients with CSNA was compared with 
that in each of two gender- and age-matched control groups. The 
first group consisted of 10 children who had undergone lumbar 
puncture for the diagnosis of a possible CNS infection, but whose 
CSF was normal. The second group consisted of 10 children who 
suffered from other neurologic developmental disorders. We also 
measured the CSF level of P-endorphin as described previouslyP 
The endogenous opiate P-endorphin acts as a neurotransmitter in 
the response to pain, in endocrine function, and in higher cortical 
 function^.^ 
The CSF level (mean t SD) of substance P was significantly 
lower in the patients with CSNA (3.12 2 2.15 fmoYmL) than in 
the first (7.27 2 1.62 fmoVmL) and second (6.82 2 1.65 fmoVmL) 
control groups (p = 0.0212, p = 0.0307, Aspin-Welch t test) (fig- 
ure). There was no significant difference between the first and the 
second control group (p = 0.5527). The CSF level of P-endorphin 
was not significantly different between patients with CSNA and 
each control group (data not shown). 
An abnormality in the nerve growth factor, re- 
quired for the normal development of sympathetic and sensory 
neurons may be a cause of hereditary sensory neuropathy. Nerve 
growth factor regulates the expression of mRNA encoding the 
precursors of substance P during early postnatal development.s In 
animal studies, there is reduced substance P staining of the spinal 
cord, especially in areas related to the sensory pathway, in an 
hereditary sensory neuropathy mf rat modeL6 In this study, we 
found a marked decrease of CSF substance P levels in patients 
with CSNA. This decreased CSF substance P level reflects a loss 
of primary sensory neurons in patients with CSNA that may be 
linked to the insensitivity to pain in this disease. 
Discussion.

Improvement of stiff-man syndrome 
with vigabatrin 
M.C. Prevett, OM; P. Brown, MD, J.S. Duncan, DM 
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare disorder characterized by 
involuntary stiffness of axial muscles with superimposed painful 
spasms, which are often precipitated by movement, startle and 
emotional stimuli.' Autoantibodies to y-aminobutyric acid 
(GABAI-ergic neurones are present in 60% of patients suggesting 
that SMS may be an autoimmune-mediated disorder.2 Benzodiaz- 
April 1997 NEUROLOGY 48 1133

epines and baclofen are the mainstays of treatment, but steroids, 
plasma exchange and intravenous human immunoglobulin may be 
useful in some  patient^.^,^ We report a patient with SMS who 
derived excellent symptomatic benefit from vigabatrin. 
Case Report. A 22-year-old woman was referred for further 
evaluation of her epilepsy. She had been well until 1989, when she 
presented acutely to her local hospital with fever, confusion and 
drowsiness. Soon after admission she developed complex partial 
seizures. Neurological examination revealed bilateral extensor 
plantar responses, but was otherwise unremarkable. Brain CT 
and CSF examination were normal. EEG showed left-sided fronto- 
temporal epileptiform activity. She was treated with carbamaz- 
epine and intravenous acyclovir. Within two weeks the fever, con- 
fusion, and drowsiness had resolved, but she was left with 
frequent complex partial seizures. 
The seizures were characterized by a gustatory hallucination 
followed by loss of awareness with lip smacking and automatic 
movements of the right hand. Neurological examination was nor- 
mal. MRI of the brain demonstrated atrophy and increased T,- 
signal in the left hippocampus, and interictal EEG showed left 
anterior temporal spikes. Carbamazepine, clobazam and sodium 
valproate failed to control the seizures, and, in June 1994, vigaba- 
trin 2 g/d was added to carbamazepine. There was a transient 
reduction in seizures, but they then returned to their usual fre- 
quency of 6 to 8 per week. 
In January 1995, the vigabatrin was discontinued and lam- 
otrigine introduced. Two months later, she noticed increasing 
back stiffness and occasional spasms affecting the trunk and legs 
without any stimulus sensitivity. The lamotrigine was discontin- 
ued in July 1995, but the stiffness and spasms persisted. In Sep- 
tember 1995, she was admitted for investigation. Further ques- 
tioning at this time revealed that a mild degree of back stiffness 
had been present for three to four years prior to the recent deteri- 
oration. On admission she was receiving only carbamazepine. Ex- 
amination showed a marked hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine 
and rigidity of the abdominal muscles. Cranial nerve examination 
was normal. Tone was increased in the legs, and the tendon re- 
flexes were brisk in the arms and legs. The abdominal reflexes 
were preserved, the right plantar response was flexor and the left 
extensor. Sensory examination was normal. EMG showed contin- 
uous motor unit activity in the axial musculature, and exterocep- 
tive reflexes, elicited from the posterior tibia1 nerve at the ankle, 
were abnormally pronounced. MRI of the spine was normal, and 
CSF examination was normal except for the presence of oligo- 
clonal IgG bands, which were not present in serum. Anti-glutamic 
acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies were strongly positive in se- 
rum. Thyroid microsomal (1/100) and gastric parietal cell antibod- 
ies were also positive. Plasma glucose, thyroid function and serum 
B,, were normal. 
Clonazepam was added and the dose gradually increased to 4 
mg/d. There was a slight reduction in the number of spasms, but 
the axial stiffness and the hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine per- 
sisted. She was unable to tolerate higher doses of clonazepam 
because of drowsiness, and in December 1995, vigabatrin was 
re-started at a dose of 0.5 g/d and increased to 2 g/d. When re- 
viewed in January 1996, the spasms had ceased and there was 
almost complete resolution of the axial stiffness and the hyper- 
lordosis of the lumbar spine. The dose of clonazepam was subse- 
quently reduced to 2.5 mg/d without exacerbation of the symp- 
toms. When reviewed four months later, she was receiving 
vigabatrin 2 g/d, slow-release carbamazepine 600 mg/d, and clon- 
azepam 2.5 mg/d. Examination revealed minimal deformity of the 
lumbar spine, and tone in the legs was normal. The tendon re- 
flexes remained brisk throughout, but both plantar responses 
were flexor. The seizures were continuing, however, unchanged. 
Discussion. We made a diagnosis of SMS on the basis of the 
axial rigidity, spasms and the typical hyperlordosis of the lumbar 
spine, in conjunction with the neurophysiological findings of con- 
tinuous motor unit activity and enhanced exteroceptive reflexes. 
Anti-GAD antibodies were strongly positive and other organ spe- 
cific autoantibodies were present supporting the diagnosis of 
SMS.3 
Seizures occur in approximately 10% of patients with SMS.5 A 
variety of seizure types may occur including generalized tonic- 
clonic seizures, “absence” seizures, and nocturnal myoclonus, but 
we are not aware of any reports of classical mesial temporal lobe 
seizures. The likely etiology of the temporal lobe epilepsy in our 
patient was the encephalitic illness in 1989, but this is not proven. 
1134 NEUROLOGY 48 April 1997 
The relationship of the SMS to the encephalitic illness is un- 
certain. The encephalitic illness and complex partial seizures may 
have been incidental to the SMS. Alternatively, the illness in 1989 
may have represented an encephalomyelitis, which subsequently 
led to the development of both the epilepsy and features of SMS. 
We are not aware of any reports of encephalitis or encephalomy- 
elitis preceding SMS, and the clinical course is not consistent with 
encephalomyelitis with rigidity, which is a relentlessly progres- 
sive disorder often with cranial nerve involvement.3 
The symptoms of SMS developed after withdrawal of vigaba- 
trin and introduction of lamotrigine. Despite discontinuing the 
lamotrigine, the symptoms persisted. There was slight improve- 
ment on clonazepam, but re-introduction of vigabatrin was associ- 
ated with striking improvement, with resolution of the spasms 
and increased tone in the legs, leaving only a mild lumbar defor- 
mity that did not interfere with walking. In retrospect, the symp- 
toms of SMS had probably been present to a mild degree for three 
to four years, and the vigabatrin had been suppressing the symp- 
toms of SMS, which only became significant following the with- 
drawal of the drug. 
The pathophysiological basis of the axial stiffness and spasms 
in SMS is uncertain. One hypothesis is that there is abnormal 
excitability of spinal interneuronal networks and their descending 
controL3 Sixty percent of patients with SMS have antibodies to 
GAD, the enzyme that converts glutamate to GABA in nerve ter- 
minah2 Benzodiazepines and baclofen, standard treatments used 
in SMS, are thought to increase GABA-ergic transmission in the 
brainstem and spinal cord;3 benzodiazepines by facilitating the 
effect of GABA at the GABA, receptor and baclofen by acting as a 
GABA, receptor agonist. Vigabatrin is an irreversible inhibitor of 
GABA transaminaseB the main metabolic route for GABA, leading 
to increased GABA levels and GABA-ergic transmission, mediated 
via both GABA, and GABA, receptors. Although vigabatrin is 
primarily used as an anti-epileptic drug, in short-term, placebo- 
controlled trials at doses of 2 to 3 g/d, it was effective in ameliorat- 
ing spasticity and reducing the frequency of spasms due to multi- 
ple sclerosis and spinal cord lesions.‘j Vigabatrin has also been 
effective as a spasmolytic agent in children with leukodystrophies 
accompanied by borderline low CSF free GABA levels.7 
There are good theoretical grounds for the observed improve- 
ment in the symptoms of SMS following treatment with vigaba- 
trin in our patient. Further evaluation in other patients with SMS 
is required, but a trial of vigabatrin may be worth considering in 
patients who have not responded to, or who are unable to tolerate, 
large doses of benzodiazepines and baclofen. In particular, vigaba- 
trin may have a role in the treatment of the 10% of patients with 
SMS who also have seizures.
